So polar calculus is not a new kind of calculus. It is parametric calculus with the angle \theta as the parameter.

The polar picture, however, gives new geometry. A small change in \theta sweeps out a small sector. A small change in r moves the point in or out along a ray. That is why the formulas for slope, area, and length look different from the ones for ordinary graphs.

exercise.title: Why is polar calculus not a new kind of calculus?

statement.p: The equation r=f(\theta) is already parametric through x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta. In your own words, why do slope, area, and length formulas then look different from the graph formulas, even though they come from the same ideas?

hint.p: Polar calculus is parametric calculus with angle as the parameter. The new look comes from sector geometry and from expressing the coordinate rates in terms of r and r'.

hint.p: Polar coordinates organize the plane by rays from the origin. Retracing, negative r, or the wrong interval can count the same region more than once.

exercise.title: Why can two polar curves meet without sharing the same r at the same \theta?

statement.p: Polar names are not unique, so the same-angle equation r_1(\theta)=r_2(\theta) can miss intersections. In your own words, what other meetings should you look for, and why does the origin need a separate check?

hint.p: Curves can meet under different angles, or both pass through the pole at different times. Nonuniqueness is useful for graphing and dangerous for solving.

subsection.title: Intersections and repeated tracing
subsection.p: Polar coordinates are not unique. That nonuniqueness is useful, but it makes intersections more delicate than in Cartesian coordinates.
Two polar curves can meet even when their equations do not give the same r at the same \theta.

note.title: Polar checklist before computing area or length
note.p: Before using a polar formula, ask:

li.p: What interval of \theta traces the desired curve?
Is the curve traced once or more than once?
Does r become negative, creating points on the opposite ray?
Does the curve pass through the origin?
If two curves intersect, are there intersections reached at different angles?

paragraphs.p: Polar coordinates are powerful because they match circular and radial geometry. But the price is that the same point may have many names.

The next family of curves makes especially good use of polar coordinates. It includes parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas. These curves can be described by distance from a fixed point and a fixed line, and in polar form they appear in one equation.

exercise.title: What should you ask before computing polar area or length?

statement.p: The section ends with a checklist: interval, repeated tracing, negative r, the origin, and hidden intersections. In your own words, why does skipping those questions turn a correct formula into a wrong geometric count?

hint.p: The formula integrates the parametrization you feed it. If the tracing is wrong, the integral is faithfully wrong.
